query: Consider the following context: Conventional material processing approaches often achieve strengthening of materials at the cost of reduced ductility. In that context, which method can be used for overcome the strength-ductility trade-off, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Implementing a heterogeneous or graded (layered) microstructure in metallic alloys will mitigate the conventional strength–ductility trade-off, enabling increased strength while preserving ductility.
generation.material_initial_state: Metal samples processed by conventional methods displaying uniform grain structure, typically showing reduced ductility when strengthened.
generation.intervention: Develop a graded or layered microstructure via a sequential forging/rolling or other thermomechanical process that locally alters grain sizes and/or phases.
generation.conditions: Perform intermediate annealing steps and use controlled temperature and strain-rate regimes during processing. Evaluate mechanical properties at or near room temperature.
generation.structural_mediator: Graded or heterogeneous grain size/phase layers across the sample thickness.
generation.mechanism: Local strain concentrations are redistributed when plastic flow occurs in heterogeneously sized or phased regions, resulting in concurrent strengthening and ductility retention.
generation.predicted_outcome: In comparison to the uniformly processed baseline, increased tensile strength occurs while ductility remains constant or improves, effectively overcoming the strength–ductility trade-off at room temperature.
generation.baseline: Uniformly processed alloys that follow the classical inverse relationship between strength and ductility, typically showing elevated strength at the expense of ductility.
generation.boundary: Excessively large gradients or phase fraction mismatches could localize strain and lead to premature failure, so appropriate gradient design and phase balance are crucial.
generation.uncertainty: Optimal choice of gradient extent, compositional distribution, and process parameters remains to be fully determined and may vary by alloy system.

falsification_experiment.design: Process two sets of samples: one with a deliberately induced gradient microstructure via sequential deformation and annealing, and one with conventional uniform microstructure. Compare their mechanical performance in uniaxial tension.
measurements: Tensile strength at yield and fracture
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If no significant improvement in ductility is observed at comparable or higher strength for samples with graded microstructure, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
High-entropy alloys (HEAs) can have either high strength or high ductility, and a simultaneous achievement of both still constitutes a tough challenge. The inferior castability and compositional segregation of HEAs are also obstacles for their technological applications. To tackle these problems, here we proposed a novel strategy to design HEAs using the eutectic alloy concept, i.e. to achieve a microstructure composed of alternating soft fcc and hard bcc phases. As a manifestation of this concept, an AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 (atomic portion) eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) was designed. The as-cast EHEA possessed a fine lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure, and showed an unprecedented combination of high tensile ductility and high fracture strength at room temperature. The excellent mechanical properties could be kept up to 700°C. This new alloy design strategy can be readily adapted to large-scale industrial production of HEAs with simultaneous high fracture strength and high ductility.

High-entropy alloys (HEAs), or multi-principal-element alloys, emerge as a new research frontier in the metallic materials community [1] [2] [3] [4] [5] [6] . HEAs differentiate with conventional alloys in th

As such, our alloy design strategy resulted in the discovery of an EHEA with a fine lamellar fcc/B2 structure and balanced high fracture strength and high ductility. This novel strategy is promising to solve the problems inhibiting the engineering application of HEAs as high-temperature materials, including the inferior castability and compositional segregation, and the conflict between high fracture strength and high ductility. In addition, this novel strategy also brought breakthrough to NiAl-based alloys in significantly enhancing the ductility at room temperature while simultaneously achieving the high strength. The EHEA concept, combining the advantages of both HEAs and eutectic alloys, and at the same time eliminating the disadvantages of these two types of alloys, leads to a promising new class of high-temperature alloys. Using this new alloy design strategy, an industrial scale HEA with uniform organizations and compositions can be prepared by the conventional casting method in a low cost way, allowing for large-scale industrial applications.
